---
title: "Research Experience"
---

My research began during my second summer at Lawrence University, when I joined Dr. Brian Piasecki's lab studying cilia function in *C. elegans*. I started by supporting a senior student's honors project—characterizing mutant phenotypes using confocal and fluorescence microscopy and dye-filling assays—before moving on to projects of my own.

Over two consecutive summers (ten weeks each) as a Lawrence University Research Fellow, I worked to generate a *mapk-15*::mCherry recombinant plasmid in order to co-localize MAPK-15 and CED-1, two proteins implicated in cilia function and neurite pruning. The first summer taught me as much through its setbacks as its successes: our Gibson Assembly construct did not yield the expected product, and the experience gave me a much deeper understanding of genetic cloning and the value of systematic troubleshooting. The following summer, with guidance from Eric Lewellyn, we pivoted to Golden Gate Assembly, which ultimately produced the recombinant plasmid we had been working toward. Seeing colonies of *E. coli* grow carrying my recombinant DNA was an enormously rewarding moment.

For my senior capstone, I am building on this work by developing annexin V staining protocols to validate a model of the CED-1 and MAPK-15 interaction in neurite pruning. While I will not have time to validate the model in full, I hope to leave the project well positioned for other undergraduate students to continue.
